provenance.method: lesson notes written from the NERDC 2025 scheme of work outline; every week keeps its scheme topic and bullets as the teaching spine

topics.title: WAEC marathon: physical chemistry
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to solve problems involving mole calculations.
The students should be able to explain energy changes in chemical reactions.
The students should be able to solve past WAEC questions on physical chemistry.

Introduction:
We have studied mole concept and energy changes in previous terms. This week we will practice WAEC questions on these topics to prepare for the exam.

Content:
Mole concept involves calculations of reactants and products in chemical reactions. For example, calculating the mass of a substance given its number of moles. Energy changes include exothermic and endothermic reactions. We will work through past WAEC questions like calculating the number of moles in 12g of carbon and determining the energy change in reactions involving common Nigerian substances like kerosene burning in stoves.

Class activity:
Students will work in groups to solve five mole calculation problems and five energy change questions from past WAEC exams.

Evaluation questions:
1. Calculate the number of moles in 18g of water.
2. Differentiate between exothermic and endothermic reactions.
3. If 2 moles of methane burn completely, how much heat is released?
4. Explain why kerosene burning in a stove is exothermic.
5. Solve: What volume of oxygen is needed to burn 1 mole of methane?

Summary:
This week we practiced mole calculations and energy changes through WAEC past questions to strengthen our exam preparation.

topics.title: WAEC marathon: inorganic
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify properties of elements in different groups.
The students should be able to explain methods of extraction of metals.
The students should be able to solve past WAEC questions on inorganic chemistry.

Introduction:
We have studied the periodic table and metal extraction in previous terms. This week we will practice WAEC questions on these topics to improve our exam technique.

Content:
The periodic table groups have characteristic properties. For example, Group I elements are highly reactive metals. Group VII elements are halogens. Methods of extraction depend on the reactivity of metals. We will work through past WAEC questions like explaining why aluminum is extracted by electrolysis while iron is extracted by reduction with carbon. We will use Nigerian examples like the extraction of iron from Ajaokuta Steel Company.

Class activity:
Students will complete a table comparing properties of elements from different groups and solve extraction problems from past WAEC papers.

Evaluation questions:
1. List two properties of Group II elements.
2. Explain why sodium is extracted by electrolysis of molten NaCl.
3. Differentiate between extraction of aluminum and iron.
4. Describe the extraction process of iron in Nigeria.
5. Why is aluminum more expensive to extract than iron?

Summary:
This week we practiced questions on periodic table groups and metal extraction to enhance our WAEC preparation.

topics.title: WAEC marathon: organic
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify different functional groups.
The students should be able to name organic compounds using IUPAC nomenclature.
The students should be able to solve past WAEC questions on organic chemistry.

Introduction:
We have studied various functional groups and naming of organic compounds. This week we will practice WAEC questions on these topics to master organic chemistry for the exam.

Content:
Organic compounds contain functional groups that determine their properties. Common functional groups include alkanes, alkenes, alcohols, carboxylic acids, and esters. Each has characteristic reactions. For example, alkenes undergo addition reactions while alcohols can be oxidized to carbonyl compounds. We will work through past WAEC questions like naming compounds with different functional groups and predicting products of reactions. We will use Nigerian examples like the production of ethanol from local crops for palm wine.

Class activity:
Students will work in pairs to identify functional groups in given compounds and name them according to IUPAC rules.

Evaluation questions:
1. Identify the functional group in CH3COOH.
2. Name the compound CH3CH2OH.
3. Differentiate between alkanes and alkenes.
4. What product is formed when ethanol is oxidized?
5. Draw the structure of butanoic acid.

Summary:
This week we practiced identifying functional groups and naming organic compounds through WAEC past questions to strengthen our organic chemistry knowledge.

topics.title: Mock examination
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to complete a full Chemistry examination under timed conditions.
The students should be able to apply knowledge across all chemistry topics.
The students should be able to identify areas of weakness for further study.

Introduction:
We have been preparing for WAEC throughout the term. This week we will take a full mock examination to simulate the actual exam experience.

Content:
The mock examination will cover all topics in the SSS 3 Chemistry curriculum including physical, inorganic and organic chemistry. It will include theory, objective and practical questions similar to WAEC format. Students will be given the full time allocation as in the actual exam. After completion, we will mark the papers and review common mistakes made by students. This will help identify areas that need more focus in our remaining preparation time.

Class activity:
Students will write a full three-hour Chemistry mock examination covering all topics in the curriculum.

Evaluation questions:
The mock examination will contain a variety of questions including:
1. Calculation of mole and concentration
2. Explanation of periodic table trends
3. Identification of functional groups
4. Description of extraction processes
5. Prediction of reaction products

Summary:
This week we conducted a full mock examination to simulate the WAEC experience and identified areas needing further attention before the actual exam.

topics.title: Practical marathon
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to perform titration experiments accurately.
The students should be able to identify salts using qualitative analysis.
The students should be able to write proper practical reports.

Introduction:
We have studied laboratory techniques and qualitative analysis throughout the term. This week we will practice these skills intensively to prepare for the practical examination.

Content:
Titration is a technique used to determine the concentration of a solution. It involves adding a solution of known concentration to a solution of unknown concentration until the reaction is complete. Qualitative analysis involves identifying cations and anions in salts through various tests. For example, testing for iron(III) ions using potassium thiocyanate solution. We will practice these techniques using common Nigerian substances like determining the concentration of acetic acid in local palm vinegar.

Class activity:
Students will perform titration experiments to determine the concentration of given solutions and carry out salt analysis to identify unknown salts.

Evaluation questions:
1. Describe the procedure for titrating sodium hydroxide against oxalic acid.
2. How would you test for the presence of chloride ions?
3. What observation indicates the presence of iron(III) ions?
4. Explain why methyl orange is used as an indicator in strong acid-strong base titrations.
5. Describe a test to distinguish between sulfate and carbonate ions.

Summary:
This week we practiced titration and salt analysis techniques to prepare for the practical examination component.

topics.title: Qualitative analysis drills
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify cations using flame tests and precipitation reactions.
The students should be able to identify anions using specific tests.
The students should be able to write balanced equations for reactions in qualitative analysis.

Introduction:
We have studied qualitative analysis in previous terms. This week we will practice fast identification of cations and anions to improve our speed and accuracy for the practical exam.

Content:
Qualitative analysis involves identifying ions in compounds through specific tests. Cations can be identified using flame tests, precipitation reactions, and complex formation tests. For example, sodium ions give a yellow flame test while copper(II) ions give a blue flame test. Anions are identified by characteristic reactions like effervescence with acid for carbonate ions or brown ring test for nitrate ions. We will practice these tests using common Nigerian substances like testing for iron in local well water.

Class activity:
Students will work in pairs to identify unknown salts by performing a series of tests on given samples and recording observations.

Evaluation questions:
1. Describe the flame test for sodium ions.
2. How would you distinguish between sulfate and sulfite ions?
3. What reagent is used to test for iron(III) ions and what is the observation?
4. Write the equation for the reaction between carbonate ions and acid.
5. Explain how to distinguish between chloride and bromide ions.

Summary:
This week we practiced fast identification of cations and anions to improve our speed and accuracy in qualitative analysis.

topics.title: Weakness clinics
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to identify their individual weak areas in chemistry.
The students should be able to explain concepts they previously found difficult.
The students should be able to solve problems in their weak areas with guidance.

Introduction:
We have completed mock examinations and identified areas of weakness. This week we will focus on these areas to improve our understanding and performance.

Content:
Each student has identified topics where they need improvement. Common weak areas include mole calculations, organic reaction mechanisms, and qualitative analysis. We will address these through targeted drills and explanations. For example, students struggling with organic reactions will practice drawing mechanisms for addition and substitution reactions. Those with difficulties in mole calculations will work through progressive examples from simple to complex. We will use Nigerian examples like calculating the amount of fertilizer needed for a small farm.

Class activity:
Students will work in small groups focusing on their identified weak areas, with the teacher providing targeted guidance and additional practice problems.

Evaluation questions:
1. Explain the concept you found most difficult and how you now understand it.
2. Solve a problem in your previously weak area.
3. Describe how you have improved in your weak area.
4. What strategies have you found helpful for understanding difficult concepts?
5. How will you continue to improve in your weak areas before the exam?

Summary:
This week we focused on individual weak areas through targeted drills to improve overall chemistry understanding.

topics.title: Speed and accuracy
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to complete objective questions within the allocated time.
The students should be able to maintain accuracy while working quickly.
The students should be able to track their progress in speed and accuracy.

Introduction:
In the WAEC examination, speed and accuracy are both crucial. This week we will practice working quickly while maintaining accuracy to improve our exam performance.

Content:
Speed and accuracy are developed through timed practice sessions. We will complete objective questions in timed conditions, gradually reducing the time allowed to build speed. Students will track their scores to monitor improvement. Common time-wasters include spending too long on difficult questions and not reading questions carefully. We will develop strategies like answering easy questions first and flagging difficult ones for later review. We will use Nigerian examples like calculating the cost of materials for a small business project.

Class activity:
Students will complete timed objective tests with questions covering all chemistry topics, tracking their scores and time taken for each test.

Evaluation questions:
1. What strategies help you work faster in chemistry exams?
2. How do you maintain accuracy when working quickly?
3. What is your average time per objective question?
4. Which types of questions take you the longest to answer?
5. How have you improved your speed and accuracy over the week?

Summary:
This week we developed speed and accuracy through timed practice sessions to improve our exam performance.

topics.title: Final mock
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to complete a full Chemistry examination under exam conditions.
The students should be able to apply knowledge across all chemistry topics effectively.
The students should be able to demonstrate improved performance compared to the first mock.

Introduction:
We have completed extensive preparation throughout the term. This week we will take our final mock examination to assess our readiness for the actual WAEC exam.

Content:
The final mock examination will be a complete WAEC-style Chemistry paper covering all topics in the curriculum. It will include theory, objective, and practical questions with the same time allocation as the actual exam. Students will write under full exam conditions without assistance. After completion, we will mark the papers and compare performance with the first mock examination to identify areas of improvement. This final assessment will help build confidence and identify any last-minute areas needing revision before the actual exam.

Class activity:
Students will write a full three-hour Chemistry mock examination under strict exam conditions.

Evaluation questions:
The final mock examination will contain a comprehensive set of questions including:
1. Complex calculations involving mole concept and stoichiometry
2. Detailed explanations of chemical principles with examples
3. Identification and naming of organic compounds
4. Description of extraction processes for various metals
5. Qualitative analysis problems with multiple steps

Summary:
This week we completed our final mock examination to assess our readiness for the WAEC Chemistry exam and identified areas for last-minute revision.

topics.title: WAEC readiness
topics.content:
Behavioural objectives:
The students should be able to explain effective exam day strategies.
The students should be able to prepare necessary materials for the examination.
The students should be able to approach the exam with confidence.

Introduction:
The WAEC examination is approaching. This week we will focus on exam day strategies and final preparations to ensure success.

Content:
Exam day strategies include proper time management, reading instructions carefully, and answering questions in order. Students should allocate time based on marks available for each question. Essential materials include calculator, mathematical tables, and required stationary. We will review common mistakes to avoid like misreading questions and poor time management. Students should arrive early at the examination center and remain calm throughout the exam. We will discuss handling the Harmattan season which might affect exam conditions in some parts of Nigeria.

Class activity:
Students will create a personal exam day checklist and participate in a group discussion on effective exam strategies.

Evaluation questions:
1. What is your strategy for managing time during the Chemistry exam?
2. List three essential materials you need for the examination.
3. How will you remain calm during difficult questions?
4. What common mistakes should you avoid in the exam?
5. Describe how you will prepare the night before the exam.

Summary:
This week we focused on exam day strategies and final preparations to ensure confidence and success in the WAEC Chemistry examination.
